title: Psalm, Job, and the Lord's Prayer prove the need of mercy
source_text: XXXII. Id manifeste docet Psaltes, Si iniquitates, inquit, observaveris Domine, Domine quis sustinebit? Psal. 130. 3. Quod Job etiam agnoscit his verbis, Vere scio quod ita sit, & quod non justificetur homo compositus Deo. Si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille. Job. 9. 2, 3. Unde est quod Propheta hac deprecatione apud Deum utitur, Et non intres in judicium cum servo tuo: quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Psal. 143. 2. Quo pertinet etiam quotidiana illa precatio, qua ex Christi praecepto, vel qui sunt inter homines sanctissimi, uti debent, Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris.
pass_a_gloss: The Psalmist teaches this plainly: If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? (Psalm 130:3). Which Job also acknowledges in these words: I know that it is so, and that a man will not be justified when compared with God. If he should wish to contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand (Job 9:2–3). Hence the Prophet uses this prayer before God: And enter not into judgment with your servant: for in your sight no living one will be justified (Psalm 143:2). To which also belongs that daily prayer which, by Christ's precept, even those who are among men the most holy ought to use: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
pass_b_english: Ps 130:3; Job 9; Ps 143:2; and the daily Our Father prove all need mercy.
Even the holiest must pray forgive us our debts.
